Were you asking what our income was or were you asking what O&G's income was? What the fees, the user fees would be for people who are going to be affected. Yes, it's like $21,000 for O&G and I think Rubino pays $7,500. I'm sorry, $5,500. $5,500, thank you. Yeah. But what about the small private boat owners and what kind of revenue? They don't pay transit fees. Oh, they don't. Okay, so it's just these commercial entities. Commercial with barges. It has to do with the barges, Sam. Okay, sorry. Well, I would be generous in some sort of partial waiver. Yeah. Mr. Chairman, what we could do is the fee, which has been fixed for a while, is based on barge and tub trips. So we know for a significant portion of one year, 2027, that that barge and tub traffic in the East Branch will either be non-existent or reduced to a trickle. And it would be much easier to count the boats and we could do many things. One of them would be an honor system by those two vendors, O&G and Rubino's, to say this is what's coming into the harbor and we can adjust it to that. So in their statement of impact, both O&G and Rubino Brothers have submitted to us statements of impact, which I have reported to the city. Rubino suggests that they ship approximately 55 barges per year of scrap metal, each holding between 800 and 1,000 tons of scrap, approximately one per week. That would equate to about 40 to 50 truckloads of outbound material. Yes. And so their impact is going to be they are charged $13 per gross ton to deliver to Jersey City where the scrap goes. The freight rate would go between $35 and $40 per gross ton. So you're looking at a three plus X cost to ship and that would be part of what their financial impact would be. And that doesn't tease out the cost to the city for all that additional traffic. Right. O&G is approximately, let's see, with a stated scale of about 1,200 tons of raw aggregate, nine barge loads of material per operating week, or, you know, 15,000 truck trips per year by land. About $105 per ton for shipping. That's a $42 million. Oh, no, sorry, that's their sales. So anyways, there's going to be significant hardship for both. Yes. Now, they pay for a harbor wide, right? They have operations at West Branch that will not be affected. So they are, you know, losing important but partial, you know, for their global facilities in Stanford. Well, as been discussed, basically the East Channel becomes the Strait of Hormuz for about four months. Is that correct, Mr. Chairman? Well, I don't know that there will be any rockets or anything like that. I certainly hope not. Yes, it will be no man's land from April until, you know, July. Okay, that's one third of the year. We could, we could, one option would be to consider, at that time, neither company pays any tug and barge fees. But it would be up to the commission to consider it and possibly approve it. Can we table this and get some more factual information? Sure. I mean, this, this, we're not going to vote on anything tonight. No, you're right. I mean, let's move on. I couldn't agree more, Mike. Thank you. All right. CHMA bill status is relatively unchanged. Cummings Marina rebuild unchanged. Stanford Greenwich Town border unchanged. Lighthouse restoration. It, I had written unchanged, but since I dropped the agenda, Gary had asked if the, if we were interested in helping with the installation costs, I'm presuming, of the, he didn't specify that, but of the internet out there. And maybe Trez can fill us in more. Trez, are you read in on all that? Is Trez still here? No, he's not. Okay. Well, so that's in the offing. He must have dropped off. But otherwise, they're still doing some restoration work to the, to the caisson. And so painting is not going to happen until either this fall or next season, apparently. Hurricane barrier closure. We got two statements of impact, both of which I have sent on to the entire team. Leah Kagan from the city, from the mayor's office has been promising to reach out to me every day of the last week and not doing so. And so that's on the mayor's. That's on the mayor's, at least, view board. Otherwise, no, no new news there. Let's see, what else do we have here? Barricade closure, Cape Park boat ramp initiative, we talked about a little bit earlier. Fund 25 unchanged. Mr. Chairman, excuse me, on that one. The Fund 25, I know you've been doing some work on our finances and our budget. We had general agreement before staffing change in the city about us investing the Fund 25. How do we get that kicked up again? Because they were going to do that. And then we had a staff change. I know Frank Fidelity knew more about this than I did. But is there a way to get that? Because we could get some money there. Yeah, so who was it that you were talking to? Frank Fidelity, are you with us? Yeah, and you had, I think, reached out to Tony Romano, correct? Tony was on board, but Tony's boss, the guy who left. Mr. McGuire? You know what, Damien, I'll touch base with you after the meeting. Yeah, okay. I mean, I'm not going to know who it was because I wasn't in on those conversations. I have some notes on that, Damien. Presumably, whoever took over for that person should be able to pick up the ball where it was dropped. When this person left. Sounds good. Okay. All right, any new business? Yeah, Mr. Chairman. This may be regarded as petty, but it really bothers me that you show up. on these teams meetings. You, Frank, Fidelity, and Jeff show up as guests. That graphic in your picture needs to be changed by our next monthly meeting. It's got to be an easy fix. Well, if it makes you feel any better, I don't see guests on the graphics, so I feel it doesn't hurt my self-esteem. Yeah, well, as I say, the three of you show up as guests, and you clearly aren't, so I think that should be fixed. I think it might be a matter of having you have to have a login set through Teams, and then it makes the whole login process easier. Yeah, well, let's get it fixed. We're not technical people here, but it's got to be fixed. It's the wrong impression. Some guest comes on and sees Dr. Ortelli guest. Come on. It's Bush League. Mike, do you have any wisdom on Teams or Maria? I think it's exactly what James was just saying. It has to do with when you go to enter. If you didn't log in and put all your credentials in, it's not going to view you as one of the commissioners, I believe. I could be wrong, Mike. I had a ton of problems logging in before I set up, and I used to log in as a guest. Right, but I think when you set yourself up, because it says right there, when you look on your name, it says this person doesn't have a Teams account. We can't verify their identity. So, if you don't log in under your Teams and create an account, then it's not verifying you. So, you're looking at as a guest. I don't. I simply copy the meeting ID, and I copy the password. That's all I do, and I come in without being a guest. I don't propose to solve it now, but somebody should be dealing with this and communicate to the group to avoid this. Okay. I mean, I don't know what more I can do other than click on my city calendar in my city Microsoft account that has the meeting time that I moved from my city. So, anyhow. Not tonight. Somebody needs to address this, though. Jeff, go ahead. I know it's late. Guys might give me just a couple minutes to talk about the hurricane barrier, because it's a very interesting situation that we're dealing with, and I think it might be described as unique. When I made my report last month about the DEP review for the coastal consistency and the water quality certification and the opportunity for public comments, we learned a couple weeks later that everything I said was wrong. And you know, back earlier, it was in the beginning of May, when we communicated with DEP, they had no knowledge of the hurricane barrier project. The Corps hadn't reached out to them, and we were their source of knowledge. And as a federal project, we assumed, and DEP told us this, that the Corps of Engineers would have to get a determination of coastal consistency from DEEP and a water quality certification, because the federal government doesn't get permits, and it's exempt from local permits and state permits. But Connecticut has a approved coastal management program, and as a result, federal activities have to be consistent with that program. So, we kept talking with DEEP, and then at the end of May, we got an email from DEEP saying that they had met with the Corps, and everything was approved. And it was approved under these new nationwide general permits that the federal government adopted earlier this year, or took effect. And you know, a general permit, like a 440 doc, is if you do something that's consistent or within the terms of the general permit, you don't have to apply for anything. You just register, and your work is approved. And so, these general permits that were established by the federal government include such things as maintenance, and discharge of materials, and so forth. And so, at the end of May, the Corps argued, the Corps of Engineers argued, that the hurricane barrier project was consistent with these general permits, and therefore didn't need any approvals from DEEP. No one knew that this was going to be applied to the hurricane barrier. So, then after that took place, we provided some additional information to DEEP, including that when DEEP makes a determination of consistency with the federal, with the Coastal Management Program, there has to be an opportunity for public comments. And then also, each one of those individual nationwide permits has a condition on the last page, that the work proposed cannot have more than an insignificant impact on navigation. And when we pointed out this to DEEP, they said that, well, we're going to have to have an additional discussion with the Corps of Engineers. But you see, and we said that if we knew that this, that those general permits were going to apply, the Corps would apply the hurricane barrier work to them, we certainly would have commented on them. But nobody knew that. So, now the question is, what is DEEP going to do? Because clearly, this has a significant impact on navigation, and we received the reports from Rubino and ONG. And Frank Baldazar did an assessment of the number of recreational boats inside the barrier, and came up with 500 recreational boats, as well as including 200 at Sezik Marina. So, clearly, there's a significant adverse impact on navigation. And how this gets worked out is going to be sort of a unique situation, because the work has to be done on the barrier. But clearly, the process didn't work the way it was intended to by the Federal Coastal Management Act and the Connecticut Act. We did not hear back from DEEP last week. And so, we'll check in with them again. But it's a real dilemma. And we'll keep pursuing it. Sorry to go on for so long, but it's quite something. Thank you. Yeah, DEEP seems like it's facing some difficult maneuvers that is impinging upon their ability to do their job from a couple of angles. And then, of course, the other response, depending on what we feel are going to be the impacts, is to discuss this with Congressman Himes's office, which has recently sent to us that they have a new infrastructure assistant who reached out to us to say that if we have any questions, we can communicate with her. She didn't mention specifically the hurricane barrier. But if the federal consistency process doesn't work, and there's substantial impacts to navigation, as well as land use impacts with truck traffic from the west to east branch, I mean, these all have to be addressed in a proper procedural way. Again, thanks. Okay. All right. Any other questions? Any other new business? Other than just to reiterate or sort of fully pronounce what Frank Fidelity was intoning, the annual cruise is August 1st. And I'm sure you all got my email today regarding that. So please RSVP, let us know if you're coming, and that way we can viddle in provision. Any other? I don't think there's anybody from the general public. Any of our esteemed shellfish committee members want to address, say anything? No? Okay. Motion to adjourn. Hang on, hang on. Next meeting is Tuesday, August 18th, 2026 at 630 in the PM. Thank you all for what you do, your time and attention tonight. Cue call. Go ahead, buddy. Motion to adjourn. Second. All in favor? Aye. Thanks, everybody. Good night, guys. Good to see y'all. Likewise.

Zoning verbiage concerning water-dependent uses.
Director Blessing was potentially going to be here tonight.
There have been a couple of emails back-and-forth about the city, as they have been, for quite
some time, sort of cleaning up their zoning books, and there was some question as to how
to define water-dependent uses, and so Jeff was kind enough to put together some verbiage,
and I wanted to give this space, if Director Blessing wanted to come and further talk it
out.
I didn't get any notification that he was going to be here, so I don't think we need
to wait for him.
But, Jeff, do you have an elevator pitch on that?
Well, I think we need to give some more thought to it, but the concern that we expressed to
Director Blessing was that, you know, a water-dependent use, a principal site use, like apartment
buildings or office buildings, we don't want that principal site use to be considered water-dependent
simply by providing public access.
And if you remember, you know, with the 14-acre site and the Davenport relocation project,
the attorney for the developer argued that boat storage and boat repair are not water-dependent
uses because you could trailer a boat to Danbury and work on it there, and that the
only true water-dependent use was public access.
But then that gets to the question of how much, but I think we want to guard against
the argument that a principal site use that's not water-dependent can be considered water-dependent
if it provides public access.
So I think that's where the, you know, we have a policy in the plan of that sort that
if there is a truly water-dependent use, marina, boatyard, boat storage, it can't be replaced
by another site use that only provides public access.
So I think, I don't know what Director Blessing's time period is, Damian, for doing this.
Perhaps if we could come up with a proposal, and I'd like to talk with Deep about it too,
because the issue is that the Connecticut Coastal Management Act, when it defines public
access, it includes uses that provide, when it defines water-dependent uses, it defines
them to include uses that provide public access.
And I think we just need to give more definition to that.
Well, and we, this might be an opportune time to remind them that in the Stanford 2035 plan,
that there was a question of starting to gradiate the water-dependent uses into categories,
right?
That was one of the major wins in that process, right?
So we can, you know, use that master plan process to start to effectuate change in the
city code.
Yes, but also if they are proposing to change the code to include these new definitions,
that proposal requires full referral to the Harbor Commission.
So we haven't seen such a referral yet.
And that would also require a referral to the DEEP.
We know what the issues are, how we deal with this in a definition, maybe we've got to see

Jeff, are you saying that you think whatever definition we come up with ultimately would

No, that is the definition of the traditional definition of a water-dependent use.
I was saying that nobody, nobody encountered it at the time.
I thought you were saying that somebody encountered it by saying that you can trailer a boat,

No, Sam, this goes way back to the boatyard, the 14-acre site, and that the applicant was

And that is what has sent us to me on this multi-decade process of trying to get gradations

I think that's a great idea.

Correct.
Yes.
But Sam...

that as opposed to a water-dependent use, maybe it's a water-use-dependent.
In other words, just simply changing that to, you need to be able to touch, feel, be

Simply seeing the water isn't a water-dependent use.
Floating, wading, touching, the transition between land and water is water-dependent.
But it depends on water.
You can see the water from a skyscraper, right?
To depend on water means you need to be able to float on it, wade in it, touch it, not
simply see it.
So instead of water-dependent use, it's water-use-dependent.
We also have to remember, Russ, we have to be consistent with the state law too, which
defines water-dependent uses.
So we're adding the purpose of zoning.
We can't diminish, change any of the state law.
We just have to add a little bit more detail to it, I think.
So here's the wrinkle.

By helping on the intake of it, are we hampering ourselves on judgment, or do we just suggest

But we can still do more research and be prepared when we do get something, you know what I

Rather than submitting it to them up front.
This is a basic question.
Yeah, I don't want to be counterproductive, you know, with something that, you know, nobody's

to judge it, to opine on it.
But, you know, I can't imagine that somebody's going to come forward and sue over that, but

If I could just add one thing, I mean, I think the damage has mostly already been done in

So, we're correct looking at, you know, the definition of what water-dependent usage is,
but that could be redefined into a kayak rack.
Yeah, hence the need to gradiate.
Yeah.

Reps to see, to take it back up again and choose differently, but not feel like they
were wrong the first time, which is, I guess, a state craft art or something, but the statesman
could.
So this person is helping to work on that, and we're hoping to get it back on agendas
and back through.
There have been some conversations in the background, answering questions, and it seems
like we've been able to turn some minds already, but there's more work to be done, but we're
not, you know, it's not going to happen this week or next week, you know, we're talking
about a couple of months, fortunately, the grant itself is a repayment grant, so we have
to front the money, and then the Port Authority will pay back, and so I don't know that, you
know, if it's sort of near to midterm timing that we may or may not, that we may not run
into a problem where the Port Authority says, all right, well, we've canceled the grant.
Jeff?
We don't have a contract yet for the grant.
I think that's one of the issues with the Port Authority, and now they're going to announce
another round of ship grants, beginning accepting applications in September 1st, and that's
for the money that wasn't spent or wasn't allocated in the first round this year, and
I know the Port Authority has asked us to give them a timeframe where the city would
have a decision as to whether to proceed with this grant, but I believe, Damian, that Erin
and someone in the Purchasing Department are communicating directly with the Port Authority
to keep them up to speed, but they did tell us it's not going to be, you know, they're
not going to hold it forever.
We needed to give them a sense of when the city would make a decision.
Well, so here's a question.
Do we need to think outside the box with this and perhaps begin the RFP process and have
the RFP process going through while we work out this back-end stuff on the payment so
that it's ready to go, and we just don't, you know, fully engage the engineers until
we know you've got this?
I don't know, and that's why we felt a little uncomfortable, you know, speaking when the
Port Authority was talking, the Port Authority Finance Director was talking with someone
in the City Finance Department who was giving them updates, but again, this is a grant that
was, this program is intended for harbor management improvement projects, which means the Harbor
Commission is the lead agency.

they did, I mean, that would be more money that they would have available to respond
to the grant applications they expect to get in September.
So I'm going to ask Aaron if we can move, reasonably move forward with the RFP process

not even the approval of the accepting of the grant, it's the approval of our budget
request to match the grant, is being metered out.
The other thing, if we were to, again, apologize for talking so much, but if we were to talk
with the Board of Reps, this application is in furtherance of the policies of the Harbor
Management Plan, which the Board of Reps has already adopted, which is to pursue opportunities
for improving public access to the harbor, and this is one of the priority projects that
we identified last year.
We do have a, you know, a slide identifying priority projects in 2025, and the one that's
been completed is our input into the comprehensive plan.
Maybe we just update, maybe there's information that we could provide to the people that are
still considering this now.
This is part of the Commission's responsibility to pursue opportunities for improving public
access to the harbor management area.
Yeah, Frank.
Mr. Chairman, I would be very cautious about adapting an RFP, a one-time RFP is a bad precedent
because it always seems to me, and I may be wrong, that the city is always trying to get
into our wheelhouse, and I don't think this would be helpful.
It's a grant.
We got the grant.
We tried to use it for a good border-dependent use, and so far, we've been unsuccessful,
but, you know, I think we've fixed that, but I'd be a little wary of that RFP process.
That's just an opinion.
Well, the RFP process takes a decent amount of time, right?
And so, what we're reacting to is that September 1st deadline that we want to make sure that
we have ourselves lined up so that this delay at Border Reps is simply that, just a delay,
and it doesn't derail, right?
And the RFP process does not, as far as I know, hinge on who or how it's going to get
paid for.
We're just requesting for proposals.
That's a good point.
You know, you don't want to miss that deadline, so I would instead suggest that that RFP,
if needed, to meet the deadline is a one-off for the time being.
And I know that...
Sometimes, it is a normal part of RFPs like that where the municipality will say that
the granting of this RFP does not mean that the project will be conducted or some sort
of a condition or disclaimer that we are not obligated to fund any or any or select any
or any or all of the proposals that we receive, that there may or may not be funding for this,
some sort of a disclaimer.
Yeah, but it will allow companies to respond so that we have an idea of what they're looking
at and then that way we're not, you know, three months to get through Board of Reps
and then another three months to get through RFP and we've blown through September significantly.
So let me send an email to Aaron and we'll see if we can get things moving in that direction.

I met with Director Quinonez and a couple of the folks from the budget side of the house
and we are looking to rework our budget mechanism in total.
We have, instead of Frank Balzar being our budget guy, but Frank doesn't have the proper
credentials so he has to go to his direct supervisor and ask for control there.
We're hoping to streamline it in-house more.
We're still going to need somebody with director level status.
This was an email that I got from Director Quinonez that I can't, as chair, I can't have
full credential control because I don't have the capability within the system, but I will
be added as a stop in the system.
So what precipitated all this was that Parks and Rec has been covering the overage from
what we have been asking for for Jeff's hard work and that ask hasn't changed in many years.
Our budget was sort of copied and pasted from year to year and of course Jeff has been
putting in more work and not getting paid what he deserves even with the overages.
And so what was happening was Parks and Rec was covering the difference, which is ridiculous.
We have funds to cover it, so we're looking to just bring our budget stuff in-house and
then that also keeps any mistakes from happening like us paying for central services and that
kind of thing.
So we're trying to learn from this budgetary shortfall thing that we found and the computing
shortfall thing that we found.
So this is a response to that.
So that's still in process, but it seems like there's going to be more control from our
end of things.
It's really taking ownership of it.
We have the capability to have an exchequer as well, right?
We have a chairman, vice chairman, a secretary, and we can also have a treasurer.
So perhaps that person, that would be a new executive board or we maybe even had one back
when I first started, I don't remember, but to have a finance in-house on the commission.
So more to come with that.

Commission, disbanded the Shellfish Commission, established the Harbor Commission as the Shellfish
Commission, and it is the current Corporation Council's opinion that that doesn't properly
give us the ability to do what the Shellfish Commission needs to do.

oh yes, the Shellfish Commission and Harbor Commission are one and the same.
And so Attorney Rosenberg's idea was to work around this, was to have an interim lease
signed by Bloom so that Bloom can be made whole, a 90-day lease while this ordinance
works its way through.
I have a meeting, much to the chagrin of Mrs. Ortelli, not my mom, my wife, well, probably
my mom as well, because we'll be on Block Island, but I am going to have to get on this
meeting on Tuesday night to defend the ordinance and make some additions to it.
And that's with the Border Reps legal committee, or whatever the heck it is.
